text: In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth.

footnotes.text: The Hebrew opens with bereshit, literally "in beginning" — without the definite article. Because of this, some read the clause as dependent: "When God began to create the heavens and the earth..." or "In the beginning of God's creating...", with verse 2 as a parenthesis and verse 3 as the main clause. The rendering here follows the long-standing reading of verse 1 as an independent sentence: a complete, self-standing declaration that stands as a title and a claim over everything that follows. This reading suits oral delivery, where the short, weighted opening line lands with full force. The pair "the heavens and the earth" is kept as a pair rather than collapsed into "the universe," since the Hebrew idiom names the two poles of creation to mean the whole of it.

Bara, "created," is a verb used in the Hebrew Bible only with God as its subject; it never takes a named material as an object. It belongs to divine action alone, unlike yatsar ("to form," as a potter) or asah ("to make"). Elohim is grammatically plural in form but takes a singular verb here (bara is third masculine singular), a standard Hebrew usage for the one God. "The heavens and the earth" is a merism — naming two extremes to include everything between them, much as "young and old" means everyone. Note also the alliteration of the opening words: bereshit bara.

The verse asserts that God precedes and originates all that exists; nothing in the created order is itself divine. If verse 1 is read as an independent declaration, it has traditionally supported the doctrine that God created out of nothing. If read as a dependent temporal clause, the text says less about the absolute beginning and more about God's ordering of the unformed world described in verse 2 — a doctrine of creation as ordering rather than origination. Both readings are ancient and both have been held within the mainstream of Jewish and Christian interpretation. Christian tradition has also heard the plural-form Elohim together with the Spirit of verse 2 and the creative word of verse 3 as an early intimation of the triune God.

The ancient Near East knew many creation accounts, several of which describe the world emerging from conflict among the gods or from the body of a defeated sea-monster. Genesis shares the vocabulary and imagery of that world — the deep, the waters, the darkness — but tells the story without rival deities and without combat. Sun, moon, sea and sky, worshipped as gods by Israel's neighbours, appear here simply as things God made.

The Hebrew tradition is remarkably stable here. Early Greek translation renders the opening as an independent clause, "In the beginning God made the heaven and the earth," using the singular "heaven"; the Hebrew shamayim is a dual/plural form. Some ancient versions and paraphrases expand the opening ("From the beginning, with wisdom, God created..."), reflecting interpretation rather than a different underlying text.

This verse opens the annual cycle of synagogue Torah readings and is chanted at the festival marking the completion and renewal of that cycle. In Christian worship it is a principal reading at the Easter Vigil, where the account of creation stands at the head of the night's rehearsal of God's saving acts, and it is widely used at services marking beginnings, thanksgiving for the created order, and the turning of the year.

text: The earth was formless and empty, darkness lay over the face of the deep, and the Spirit of God hovered over the face of the waters.

versions.text: The earth was formless and empty, and darkness lay over the face of the deep, while the Spirit of God hovered over the face of the waters.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew uses three coordinated clauses joined by simple 'and' (waw), with no subordinating sense. Rendering the last clause with 'while' subordinates it and slightly weakens the solemn, parallel cadence of the opening. Dropping the first 'and' and beginning the final clause with 'and' restores the balanced three-beat rhythm that reads well aloud, while keeping 'the face of the deep' / 'the face of the waters' parallel as in the original.

footnotes.text: The verse opens with a Hebrew construction (conjunction plus noun before the verb) that marks a break in the narrative flow: rather than reporting the next event, it describes the state of affairs. Some render it "Now the earth was..." to bring this out; the rendering here keeps the flow natural for reading aloud while letting the three clauses stand as three parallel snapshots. The verb translated "was" (hayetah) is the ordinary verb of being; a few interpreters have proposed "became" (implying a ruin between verses 1 and 2), but the grammar of a descriptive clause like this favors "was." The pair tohu wa-bohu is notoriously hard to capture; "formless and empty" is one of several possibilities alongside "a trackless waste and emptiness" or "welter and waste." The verb merachefet is rendered "hovered" rather than "swept" or "was moving," and ruach Elohim as "the Spirit of God" rather than "a wind from God" (see the notes on language and theology). "Lay over the face of" and "over the face of" preserve the Hebrew idiom "upon the face of," which gives the line its slow, measured cadence.

Tohu wa-bohu is a rhyming word-pair, and bohu occurs in the Hebrew Bible only in company with tohu; the effect is close to English phrases like "helter-skelter" — sound reinforcing sense. Tohu alone can mean desert waste, nothingness, or futility. Tehom, "the deep," is a poetic term for the primeval ocean, cognate with Akkadian tiamtu/tâmtu ("sea"); it takes no article here, functioning almost as a name. Ruach carries the whole range "breath, wind, spirit," and Elohim can be read as a genitive ("of God") or, in some idioms, as a superlative ("a mighty wind"), which is why interpreters differ. The participle merachefet describes ongoing action; the same root is used of an eagle fluttering protectively over its young (Deuteronomy 32:11) and, in a related Semitic usage, of a bird gliding — hence "hovered" rather than "brooded" or "rushed."

Two readings of ruach Elohim have long coexisted. Read as "the Spirit of God," the line becomes a foundational text for the Spirit's role in creation, echoed in passages that speak of God's breath giving life and renewing the earth, and drawn on in Christian trinitarian reflection on creation as the work of Father, Word, and Spirit. Read as "a wind from God" or "a mighty wind," the clause simply describes God's power stirring over the chaos. Ancient and modern interpreters are found on both sides. A further question is whether verse 2 describes raw material God had just made (verse 1 as the first act) or a state of unformed chaos that the following days order and fill; the six days that follow do proceed by first giving form and then filling it, answering "formless" and "empty" in turn. Notably, the darkness and the deep are described without hostility here: unlike neighboring myths, there is no battle, only God's presence over the waters.

Ancient Near Eastern cultures widely pictured the world's beginning in terms of primeval waters and darkness; Mesopotamian tradition personified the salt sea as the goddess Tiamat, and Egyptian accounts spoke of the primordial waters of Nun. The Hebrew tehom is linguistically related to that shared Semitic vocabulary for the deep, but here it is stripped of divinity: no gods contend, and the waters are simply part of the scene over which God's Spirit moves. For an audience familiar with those stories, this quiet opening would have sounded like a deliberate contrast.

The Hebrew text of this verse is stable across the manuscript tradition, including the scroll evidence from the Judean desert. Early translations show interpretive rather than textual differences: the ancient Greek version renders tohu wa-bohu as "unseen and unformed," and the early Aramaic paraphrases variously read the ruach as "a wind from before the Lord" or "a spirit of mercy from God," reflecting the same ambiguity discussed above. The Greek verb chosen for merachefet suggests being borne along over the waters.

This verse belongs to the great creation reading traditionally used at the vigil of Easter and at other services marking new beginnings, where the Spirit hovering over the waters is heard alongside the waters of baptism. It is also widely used in blessings of water and in prayers invoking the Spirit.

text: And God said, "Let there be light," and there was light.

footnotes.text: The Hebrew is famously terse — four words, then two: "yehi 'or, wayhi 'or." The translation keeps that compactness rather than expanding it, and preserves the opening "And" (Hebrew waw-consecutive) because the whole chapter is built as a chain of linked clauses meant to be heard, not merely read. "Let there be light" renders a jussive verb, a form of command or wish; alternatives such as "Light, be!" or "Let light exist" are defensible but sound clipped or abstract when read aloud. The closing clause repeats the same two words in the same order, so the English deliberately echoes it: light spoken, light there. Quotation marks are an English convention; Hebrew has none, marking speech only with the verb "said."

The command and its fulfillment are nearly identical in Hebrew: yehî 'ôr ("let there be light") is answered by wayhî 'ôr ("and there was light") — the same root h-y-h, the same consonants, with only the narrative prefix added. The effect is that speech and event are almost the same sound. Note also that the word here is 'ôr, ordinary light, while the sun, moon, and stars in verse 14 are called me'orot, "light-bearers" or lamps — luminaries formed from the same root but clearly distinguished from the light of day one.

This is the first divine speech in Scripture and the pattern for the whole chapter: God creates by word alone, without struggle, material, or assistant. Later tradition drew heavily on this — creation through the word, and the light of the first day as a sign of God's self-revelation. Christian readers have connected it to the Word through whom all things were made and to the God who "said, let light shine out of darkness." Jewish tradition long puzzled over light existing three days before the sun, some holding that this primordial light was hidden away for the righteous, others that the luminaries merely became the vessels of a light already made. The verse also asserts that light is created, not divine — a quiet refusal of any worship of sun or dawn.

In the surrounding cultures of the ancient Near East, creation was often told as combat or craftsmanship: a storm-god defeating a chaos-monster, a potter shaping clay. Creation by pure utterance was known — Egyptian theology from Memphis described the god Ptah bringing things into being by thought and speech — but here it is total and unopposed. Sun, moon, and dawn were major deities across Mesopotamia, Egypt, and Canaan; the placement of light on the first day, well before the heavenly bodies, sets this account apart from those cosmologies.

The verse is textually stable across the Hebrew manuscript tradition, the Samaritan Pentateuch, and the Dead Sea Scroll fragments of Genesis. The ancient Greek version renders the jussive with an imperative form and the result with a simple past, matching the Hebrew closely; some later Greek witnesses shift material from verse 4 forward, but no variant affects the sense of the command itself.

These words open the first reading of the Easter Vigil in many Christian traditions, where the creation of light is heard in a darkened church lit only by candles. In Jewish daily morning prayer, the blessing before the Shema praises the God "who forms light and creates darkness," drawing together this verse and the words of Isaiah.

text: God saw that the light was good, and he separated the light from the darkness.

footnotes.text: The Hebrew literally reads "And God saw the light, that (it was) good" — the object comes first, then a clause commenting on it. English idiom prefers "God saw that the light was good," which is what the translation adopts for smooth oral delivery. Some render the construction with an exclamatory force, "God saw how good the light was," which captures the note of approval but is harder to read aloud in sequence with the following clause.

Hebrew names God twice in this verse ("God saw... God separated"); the translation keeps the first and uses "he" for the second, since repeated proper nouns sound heavier in English than in Hebrew, where such repetition is normal narrative style. Likewise the Hebrew says "made a division between the light and between the darkness"; the translation uses the natural English pattern "separated the light from the darkness."

The word rendered "good" (tov) covers what is beautiful, fitting, beneficial and working as intended — not primarily a moral verdict. The verb rendered "separated" (hivdil) is causative, "to make a division," and the Hebrew idiom repeats the preposition "between... and between." The same verb later describes the distinctions a priest must teach: between holy and common, clean and unclean.

Two acts define God's work here: evaluation and separation. Creation proceeds not only by speaking things into being but by ordering them, drawing boundaries that make life possible. Notably the light is called good while the darkness is not condemned — it is given a place and later a name, which sets this account apart from dualistic systems where darkness is an evil rival power. Later writers draw on this verse when they speak of light shining in darkness and of God who says "Let light shine" in human hearts.

In the cosmologies of the surrounding cultures, light typically radiated from divine beings or from the sun and other heavenly bodies. Here light exists and is evaluated before the luminaries are made on the fourth day, and the sun and moon are later presented as appointed lamps rather than deities — a pointed contrast with the astral religion of the ancient Near East.

The Hebrew manuscript tradition is stable for this verse. The ancient Greek translation renders "good" with a word meaning "beautiful, fine," reflecting the breadth of the Hebrew term, and reproduces the doubled "between" of the Hebrew idiom.

This verse belongs to the creation reading that traditionally opens the great vigil before Easter, and its imagery of light divided from darkness has long shaped evening lamp-lighting prayers and hymns.

text: God called the light day, and the darkness he called night. And there was evening, and there was morning—the first day.

footnotes.text: The Hebrew reads literally "day one," using the cardinal number *echad* rather than the ordinal *rishon* ("first") that would be expected, and which is in fact used for the following days from day two onward ("a second day," "a third day"). Rendering it "the first day" follows the sense of the counting sequence and reads smoothly aloud; "one day" or "day one" are equally defensible and preserve the oddity of the Hebrew, which may mark this day as unique — the day when time itself begins. The clause order in the second half of the first sentence has been kept as in Hebrew ("and the darkness he called night"), reproducing the mirrored, chiastic arrangement of the original rather than flattening it to "and he called the darkness night." The dash before "the first day" stands in for a Hebrew construction with no connecting word, where the closing phrase simply sits alongside what precedes it as a summary.

The verb *qara* means both "to call" and "to name," and with the preposition *le* ("to/for") it means "to give a name to." The two halves of the naming form a chiasm: verb–subject–object–name / object–verb–name, a common Hebrew way of binding a pair of statements into a single balanced unit. Note also that God names day, night, sky, earth, and seas — the great cosmic realms — while the naming of the animals is later handed over to the human being. The repeated *wayehi* ("and there was") echoes the *yehi* ("let there be") of verse 3, so that command and outcome are joined by the same verb.

In the ancient Near East, to name something was to assert authority over it and to assign it a place and function in the ordered world. By naming light and darkness, God is portrayed not merely as their maker but as their sovereign: even the darkness, which is not called "good," is given a name and a bounded time, and so belongs within the order of creation rather than standing outside it as a rival power. The rhythm of evening and morning also establishes measured, bounded time as a creature of God — the first thing to be structured after light itself.

"And there was evening, and there was morning" reflects the Israelite reckoning of the day as beginning at sunset rather than at dawn or midnight. This convention shapes the observance of the Sabbath and the festivals, which begin in the evening of the preceding calendar date, and it continues in Jewish practice to the present.

The Masoretic text closes the verse with a *petuchah* marker (פ), a scribal sign indicating an open paragraph break — the end of the first day's account. Ancient versions render *yom echad* variously; the early Greek translation preserves the cardinal form ("day one"), while some later versions harmonize it with the ordinals of the following days.

This verse concludes the first of the seven creation-day units that structure the opening chapter and that have long shaped the liturgical reading of Genesis at vigils, at the Easter vigil in particular, and in evening prayer traditions that mark the day's turning at nightfall in accordance with the pattern of evening preceding morning.

text: And God said, "Let there be a vault in the midst of the waters, and let it separate water from water."

versions.text: And God said, "Let there be a vault in the midst of the waters, to separate water from water."
versions.explanation: The Hebrew has a second jussive ("and let it be separating"), a parallel command rather than a purpose clause. Rendering it as "and let it separate" preserves the two-part structure of the divine word and gives a better oral cadence with the balanced clauses.

footnotes.text: "Vault" renders Hebrew raqia, a term for the expanse of sky conceived as a solid, arching structure. Other renderings include "firmament," "dome," "expanse," and simply "sky." "Firmament" preserves the sense of something firm but has become archaic; "expanse" loses the connotation of solidity that the Hebrew word carries. "Vault" was chosen as a single, easily spoken word that suggests both an arch overhead and something built. The verse ends with the compact Hebrew phrase "between water and water"; the rendering "separate water from water" keeps the same brevity while reading smoothly aloud. The verb translated "let there be" and "let it separate" is the same form used in verse 3, so the divine command here echoes the first act of creation.

Raqia derives from the root raqa, used of hammering or beating out metal into thin sheets (compare the beaten metal plates of Exodus 39:3 and Numbers 16:38). The noun therefore evokes something stretched or spread thin like hammered metal. The two verbs are jussives, a Hebrew form expressing a command or wish in the third person: "let it be." The participle mavdil, "separating," is the same verb used in verse 4 when God separated light from darkness, marking division as the pattern of these creation days. The word tokh, "midst," denotes the middle or inside of something, so the vault comes into being within a single body of water that is thereby split in two.

In the shared cosmology of the ancient Near East, the visible sky was pictured as a solid canopy holding back an ocean above, which explained rain, and resting over the earth with the seas and subterranean waters below. This picture appears elsewhere in the Hebrew Scriptures, for example in the windows or floodgates of heaven in the flood narrative. Understanding this background helps explain why the text speaks of waters above the sky as well as below it.

The creation account presents God bringing order out of watery chaos by acts of separation rather than by combat, in contrast to neighboring myths in which the sky is formed from the body of a defeated sea deity. Here the waters are neither divine nor hostile; they simply obey. Interpreters differ on how the ancient picture of a solid sky relates to modern cosmology: some read these verses as describing the world in the observational language of the original hearers, others as phenomenological description of the visible sky, and others as intentionally shaped to declare God's sovereignty over the forces that pagan neighbors worshiped.

Some ancient witnesses, including the Greek translation, add "and it was so" at the end of this verse, matching the pattern of the other creation commands and anticipating the same phrase at the close of verse 7. The traditional Hebrew text does not include it here, and the translation follows that reading.

text: So God made the vault and separated the water under the vault from the water above it. And it was so.

footnotes.text: The Hebrew opens with a narrative verb form, wayya'as, literally "and God made." Rendering it "So God made" ties the deed to the command of the previous verse: what God speaks, God does. The Hebrew then spells the phrase out in full — "between the waters that were under the vault and between the waters that were above the vault" — repeating both "waters" and "vault." For oral reading this fourfold repetition is heavy in English, so the second half is shortened to "from the water above it," keeping the sense while letting the sentence breathe. "Water" is kept singular in English, though the Hebrew noun is grammatically plural, since English "waters" sounds archaic in ordinary speech. "Vault" translates raqia', a solid arched expanse; older renderings use "firmament," and some prefer "expanse" or "dome." The closing wayehi-khen, "and it was so," is a refrain of the creation account confirming that the command was carried out exactly.

The verb 'asah ("make, do, work") is broader than bara' ("create") used in verse 1; it is the ordinary word for fashioning or accomplishing something, and the two verbs alternate throughout the chapter without any sharp doctrinal distinction. The noun raqia' derives from the root raqa', "to beat out, hammer flat," used elsewhere of overlaying metal into thin sheets — hence the image of a beaten-out canopy. The verb hivdil, "separate, divide," is the same causative used of light and darkness in verse 4 and later of Israel's separations of clean from unclean, making division a key creative act. Mayim, "water," appears only in a plural form in Hebrew and takes plural agreement, much like English "waters" but with no singular counterpart.

The picture assumed here is the shared cosmology of the ancient Near East: a flat earth beneath a solid sky-vault, with a heavenly ocean held above it and subterranean waters below. Rain, in this view, comes through openings in the vault — an image used explicitly in the flood narrative. Neighbouring creation stories describe a comparable splitting of a primeval sea, though there the waters are a defeated deity; here they are simply material that God orders by his word. The account describes the world as it appears to the eye and as ancient hearers imagined it, not as a technical cosmography.

Creation here proceeds by separation rather than by conflict: God does not battle the chaotic waters but assigns them boundaries. This ordering of habitable space anticipates days four through six, when the separated realms are filled. Interpreters have long noticed that day two alone lacks the refrain "and God saw that it was good." Some rabbinic readings connect this to the work of division being incomplete until the waters below are gathered on the third day, where "good" is then said twice; others see a reticence to pronounce good a day devoted to splitting apart. Later theology read the passage as testimony that even the heavens are creatures, not divine powers.

The Masoretic text places "and it was so" at the end of this verse; the ancient Greek tradition places it at the end of verse 6, after the command, and correspondingly reshapes the report of its fulfilment. The Greek also supplies "and God saw that it was good" for the second day, filling the gap left in the Hebrew — most likely a harmonizing addition to match the other days rather than an older reading. Some Greek witnesses attach that clause to verse 8 instead. The Hebrew wording of the verse itself is stable across the manuscript evidence.

text: And God called the vault the heavens. And there was evening, and there was morning—the second day.

versions.text: God called the vault heaven. And there was evening, and there was morning—the second day.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew שָׁמָיִם is rendered "the heavens" in the following verse ("the waters under the heavens"), so naming it "heaven" here creates an inconsistency in the naming formula that a listener would notice when the two verses are read aloud together. Adding the initial connective "And" also matches the narrative chain of the surrounding verses and gives the sentence a smoother spoken cadence.

footnotes.text: The naming formula in Hebrew uses a preposition: God "called to the vault, 'Heavens.'" English cannot easily mirror this, so the standard double-object construction "called the vault the heavens" is used. The noun shamayim is grammatically plural (dual in form), and "the heavens" preserves that shape while also matching the wording of the next verse, "the waters under the heavens." A rendering such as "Sky" is equally defensible and reads more naturally as a proper name, but it obscures the link to verse 9 and to the plural expression "heavens and earth" in verse 1. The closing line keeps the fixed refrain of the creation week word for word — "And there was evening, and there was morning" — with an em dash before "the second day," which lets a reader pause naturally and lands the phrase as the day's seal rather than as a subordinate clause.

Shamayim occurs only in the plural/dual form; no singular is attested in Biblical Hebrew. Its ending (-ayim) resembles that of paired things (hands, eyes) and of mayim, "waters" — a resonance that is hard to miss in a verse where the vault is precisely what holds waters apart. Ancient interpreters played on this, deriving shamayim from sham mayim, "there is water," or from esh u-mayim, "fire and water." These are folk etymologies rather than historical derivations; the word is more likely related to a Semitic root for "be high" and has cognates across Akkadian and Ugaritic. Note also the verb form: the naming verb takes the preposition le-, a construction used throughout this chapter (verses 5, 8, 10) for the divine acts of naming.

Naming is an exercise of authority in the Hebrew Bible: to name is to assign place and function. By naming light, darkness, the vault, the dry land and the seas, God claims each domain. This is quietly polemical. In the surrounding cultures the sky was itself a deity or the body of a defeated god; here it is a manufactured object that receives its name from its maker. Interpreters have long noticed that the second day alone lacks the verdict "and God saw that it was good" — some read this as significant (the work of separation is completed only on day three, when the waters below are gathered), others as simply a feature of the text's structure, with the double approval on day three compensating.

Ancient Near Eastern cosmology commonly pictured the sky as a solid expanse holding back a cosmic ocean, with openings or windows through which rain could fall (compare the "windows of the heavens" in the flood narrative). The waters above the vault in verses 6-8 reflect this shared picture of the world. What is distinctive here is not the cosmology but its demythologizing: the upper waters are not a hostile monster to be subdued in battle but simply water, put in its place by a word.

The Greek tradition adds at the end of this verse "and God saw that it was good," regularizing the pattern of the creation week; it correspondingly places "and it was so" at the end of verse 6 rather than verse 7. The Hebrew tradition is uniform in lacking the approval formula on the second day, and the shorter reading is generally preferred as original, the Greek plus being an obvious harmonization. The Hebrew text also marks a paragraph break after this verse, closing off the second day as a unit.

text: And God said, "Let the waters under the heavens be gathered into one place, and let the dry ground appear." And it was so.

footnotes.text: The verb rendered "be gathered" is a passive (niphal) form; it could also be read reflexively, "let the waters gather themselves." The passive keeps the focus on God's word as the agent, matching the pattern of the other creation commands. "Dry ground" translates a single Hebrew noun that means precisely the dry part of the earth; it is rendered "dry ground" rather than "dry land" so that the following verse can name it "land" without the sentence sounding circular. "Into one place" is literal; the Hebrew phrase can also be heard as "to one gathering-place," which is how some ancient readers took it. The closing "And it was so" is a short formula that recurs through the chapter and is kept identical each time for the ear.

The verb for gathering (qawah) shares its root with the noun miqweh, "reservoir, gathered mass," which appears in the next verse for the sea; the command and its fulfillment are bound together by sound. The same consonants also form a homonym meaning "to wait, to hope," a coincidence later Jewish readers enjoyed but which is not the sense here. "Dry ground" (hayyabbashah) comes from a root meaning "to be dry, to wither"; the same word describes the seabed laid bare at the crossing of the sea, so that Israel's rescue is told in the language of creation.

The ancient Greek version reads "into one gathering" rather than "into one place," and adds an extended fulfillment clause: "And the water under heaven was gathered into its gatherings, and the dry land appeared." This longer form matches the report-after-command pattern found on the other days, and a fragmentary scroll from the Judean desert appears to support a similar reading. It is uncertain whether the shorter Hebrew text was expanded for symmetry or the longer text was shortened; the translation follows the traditional Hebrew wording.

On this day nothing new is made; what exists is sorted and given boundaries. Creation here is the ordering of chaos rather than production from nothing, and the sea is not a rival power but water that goes where it is told. Later texts celebrate this same act as God setting a limit the waters may not cross, so that the stability of dry ground is a daily mercy rather than a given. Readers have also seen a pattern: the separations of days one to three prepare the spaces that days four to six will fill.

Other ancient Near Eastern accounts also picture the world beginning as water, with land rising as a mound out of the deep; in Egyptian tradition the primeval hill emerges from the waters of Nun, and in Mesopotamian texts the sea is a divine antagonist. This account shares the imagery of emerging land but not the combat: there is no struggle, only a command. For farmers and shepherds in a land dependent on seasonal rain, the boundary between fertile ground and destructive water was an everyday concern, not an abstraction.

text: And God called the dry ground land, and the gathered waters he called seas. And God saw that it was good.

versions.text: God called the dry ground land, and the gathered waters he called seas. And God saw that it was good.
versions.explanation: The surrounding verses render the waw-consecutive chain with an initial connective ("And God said...", "And it was so"). Opening this verse with "And God called" preserves the cadence of the creation narrative and gives the sentence a smoother rhythm when read aloud. The rest of the verse is accurate: "the gathered waters" faithfully renders miqweh ha-mayim, and "land" keeps 'erets consistent with verse 11.

footnotes.text: The Hebrew noun *erets* can mean "earth" (the whole world), "land" (a region), or "ground." Here it is rendered "land" both because it is set in contrast to the seas rather than to the heavens, and because the same word must carry over naturally into the next verse, "Let the land bring forth." "Earth" is a defensible alternative and is common, but it risks suggesting the planet as a whole rather than the newly exposed dry surface. The phrase *miqweh hammayim*, literally "the gathering of the waters" or "the collection place of the waters," is compressed to "the gathered waters" for the sake of oral rhythm; a fuller rendering would be "the place where the waters were gathered." The plural *yammim* is kept as "seas." The closing clause *ki-tov* has no expressed subject or verb — literally "that good" — so "that it was good" supplies what English requires; the repeated refrain is deliberately worded identically throughout the chapter so that a listener hears it as a refrain.

The verse is bound to the preceding one by sound: *yiqqawu* ("let them be gathered," v. 9) and *miqweh* ("gathering, reservoir") come from the same root q-w-h. The word *miqweh* later became the technical term for a pool of gathered water used for ritual immersion. *Yabbashah*, "dry ground," is built on the root y-b-sh, "to be dry," and there is a further play in the pairing of *yabbashah* with *yammim*, "seas." The idiom "call X to Y" (*qara le-... Y*) is the standard naming formula and marks the namer as the one with authority over what is named. The plural "seas" may be a true plural (the various bodies of water known to the ancient world) or a plural of extent describing the single world-ocean.

Naming in the biblical world is an act of sovereignty and ordering, not merely of labeling. By naming the sea, God brings under His authority the very element that ancient cultures feared as untamed. Notably, this is the second declaration of "good" on the third day (the first of the two days that receive it twice), which some read as marking the completion of the work of separation begun on day one. The pronouncement over the sea is also significant: what is elsewhere in Scripture an image of chaos and threat is here declared good, part of a creation that is ordered and blessed by its Maker.

In the surrounding cultures of the ancient Near East, the sea was often personified as a hostile deity — Yam in Ugaritic texts, Tiamat in Mesopotamian tradition — subdued in combat by a warrior god before the world could be made. Here there is no combat and no rival: the sea is simply a body of water that God gathers, names, and approves. The absence of struggle is itself a statement, and the plain noun *yammim* stands where a proper name might have stood.

The Hebrew text of this verse is stable in the manuscript tradition. The Masoretic text places a vertical stroke (paseq) after "God," a scribal mark of separation with no effect on the sense. The ancient Greek version renders the gathered waters with a plural noun, "gatherings/systems of waters," reflecting the same consonantal text.

As part of the opening creation account, this verse belongs to a passage read at Easter Vigil services and at other celebrations of creation, where the naming of land and sea leads into the blessing of the earth's fruitfulness in the verses that follow.

text: Then God said, "Let the land bring forth green growth: seed-bearing plants and fruit trees, each bearing fruit with seed in it, according to its kind, upon the land." And it was so.

versions.text: Then God said, "Let the land bring forth green growth: seed-bearing plants and fruit trees on the land, each bearing fruit with seed in it, according to its kind." And it was so.
versions.explanation: The phrase "on the land" currently interrupts the pair "seed-bearing plants and fruit trees" and sits close to the earlier "the land," creating an awkward echo when read aloud. Placing it at the close of the clause matches the Hebrew word order ("upon the earth" stands at the end) and gives the line a smoother cadence before "And it was so."

footnotes.text: The Hebrew opens with a cognate construction, tadshe' ha'arets deshe' — literally "let the land grass grass" or "let the land sprout sprouting." Since English has no verb built on "green growth," the rendering "let the land bring forth green growth" keeps the sense while preserving the noun; "vegetate vegetation" or "sprout sprouts" would be more literal but stilted for reading aloud. The colon reflects a common reading of the syntax in which deshe' is a general heading and the two following items — seed-bearing plants and fruit trees — spell out what that growth consists of; an alternative reading takes them as three parallel categories ("green growth, plants, trees"). "Each bearing fruit with seed in it, according to its kind" renders 'oseh peri lemino asher zar'o-vo, with the phrase order lightly adjusted so the rhythm carries. "Upon the land" translates 'al-ha'arets, which in Hebrew stands at the end and most naturally modifies the whole act of sprouting; it is kept in final position here. 'Erets is rendered "land" for consistency with the naming in verse 10, though "earth" is equally possible.

Three plant terms appear: deshe', fresh green shoots or new growth of the kind that appears after rain; 'esev, low plants and herbage, often those useful to humans and animals; and 'ets peri, literally "tree of fruit," further specified as 'oseh peri, "making fruit." The participle mazri'a zera' ("seeding seed") is another cognate pairing, matching the verb-plus-noun play at the start of the verse; the whole line is knit together by sound as much as by sense. Min, "kind" or "species," is a broad classificatory word, not a technical biological term; the suffix in lemino is singular ("its kind"), distributed over each type, while verse 12 uses the plural sense "their kinds."

God does not make the plants directly but summons the land to produce them: creation here is mediated, with the newly named land given a generative role under the divine word. The stress on seed marks the vegetation as self-perpetuating, equipped to continue without further acts of creation. Unlike light, sky, land and seas, the plants receive no name from God, and unlike the creatures of days five and six they are never called living beings (nephesh); in this account vegetation belongs to the ordered furnishing of the world rather than to its animate life. The repeated "according to its kind" underlines an ordered, differentiated world rather than a formless fertility, an implicit rejection of the divinized fertility powers worshipped by Israel's neighbors. Readers have long noticed that plants appear on day three, before the sun on day four — a sequence that puts the life of the world in the hands of God's word rather than of the heavenly bodies.

The two categories named match the staples of life in the ancient Levant: field crops sown from grain ("seed-bearing plants") and orchard produce such as olive, fig, date, pomegranate and vine ("fruit trees"). In a rain-dependent agricultural society, the sudden greening of the ground after the first rains was the most vivid image available for the land coming to life, and deshe' is the word used for exactly that. The interest in seed within the fruit reflects practical knowledge of propagation: what a farmer plants and what an orchard keeper preserves for the next planting.

Several ancient witnesses, including the Samaritan Pentateuch and the early Greek tradition, add "according to its kind" after the seed-bearing plants, bringing this verse into line with verse 12, where the phrase appears with both categories. The Hebrew text preserved by the Masoretes has the phrase only once, with the trees, and that shorter reading is followed here as the more likely original, the longer one being an easy harmonization. The Greek tradition also expands the description of the plants somewhat and adds a clause anticipating the fulfillment in verse 12.

text: The land brought forth green growth: seed-bearing plants, each according to its kind, and trees bearing fruit with seed in it, each according to its kind. And God saw that it was good.

versions.text: The land brought forth green growth: seed-bearing plants according to their kinds, and trees bearing fruit with seed in it, according to their kinds. And God saw that it was good.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew לְמִינֵהוּ is singular ("according to its kind"), and verse 11 already renders it that way. Using "each according to its kind" keeps the wording consistent with the preceding verse, matches the singular "with seed in it," and reads more smoothly aloud with the paired phrases balancing each other.

footnotes.text: The Hebrew verb here (a causative form of "go out") differs from the verb in the command of verse 11 ("let the land sprout"); rendering it "brought forth" keeps the echo of the command while marking the shift from summons to result. The three nouns "green growth: seed-bearing plants... and trees" stand side by side without a connecting word in Hebrew after the first; the colon treats "green growth" as the general heading and the plants and trees as its two specifics, an alternative being to list all three in series ("green growth, plants... and trees"). "Each according to its kind" translates a single Hebrew word repeated twice; here it attaches to both the plants and the trees, whereas in verse 11 it was linked to the trees only, so the report fills out what the command left implicit. The final clause has no expressed object in Hebrew—literally "and God saw that good"—so "that it was good" supplies the verb English requires. The short, balanced clauses and the deliberate repetition of "each according to its kind" are kept for the sake of reading aloud.

"Seed-bearing" renders a causative participle, literally "making seed to sprout"—vegetation that carries within itself the means of its own renewal. The wording plays on sound as well as sense: the noun for "green growth" and the verb of sprouting share the same root, an effect close to "the land greened with greenery." The word translated "kind" is a Hebrew noun of uncertain etymology that occurs almost exclusively in the creation account and in later lists of clean and unclean creatures; the suffix on it is singular ("its kind"), distributing across the whole class rather than naming one species.

This verse is the classic fulfilment report: what God speaks in verse 11 comes about exactly in verse 12, and the divine word is shown to be effective without remainder. Notably the land itself is the agent that brings the vegetation out, an instance of mediated creation in which a creature is granted a share in producing life. The self-seeding capacity described here is often read as the first hint of the blessing of fruitfulness later spoken over animals and humans: creation is equipped to continue. The verdict "good" concerns fitness and ordered goodness—the world working as intended—rather than moral virtue; and it is pronounced over the vegetation itself, not merely over the process. Interpreters have long debated whether "kinds" implies fixed boundaries between living forms; the term functions in the text as ordered variety within a good creation rather than as a technical biological claim.

For "trees bearing fruit" some ancient witnesses, including the Samaritan tradition and the early Greek version, read a fuller phrase matching verse 11 ("fruit trees bearing fruit"), a natural harmonisation of report to command; the shorter Hebrew reading followed here is likely original, since scribes tended to expand toward the parallel rather than trim it. The Greek version also distributes the phrase "according to its kind" somewhat differently across verses 11 and 12 and adds "and according to its likeness" in places, reflecting an attempt to smooth the same tension the Hebrew leaves standing.

The categories used here reflect the everyday classification of an agrarian society rather than a scientific taxonomy: low ground cover, field plants grown from saved seed, and orchard trees such as fig, olive, pomegranate and date. Seed saved from one harvest for the next was a household's guarantee of survival, so the emphasis on plants "with seed in it" would have carried immediate practical weight for the first hearers. Comparable creation accounts from the ancient Near East rarely dwell on vegetation in this ordered way; the interest here is in a dependable, food-yielding world.

text: And there was evening, and there was morning—the third day.

footnotes.text: The verse repeats word for word the refrain that closes each creation day, and the translation deliberately keeps it identical in English so that the reader hears a recurring cadence rather than fresh wording. The verb וַיְהִי is rendered "and there was" (literally "and it came to be"), and the twofold "and there was" preserves the Hebrew repetition instead of compressing it to "there was evening and morning." The dash before "the third day" replaces no Hebrew word: the Hebrew simply juxtaposes the day-count with no verb or conjunction, and a dash reproduces that abrupt summarizing effect better than "that was" or a comma. Hebrew has no definite article on יוֹם שְׁלִישִׁי, so a strictly literal rendering would be "a third day"; "the third day" is preferred here because English counting idiom expects the article and because the sequence is a fixed series.

עֶרֶב ("evening") and בֹקֶר ("morning") name the two boundary moments of the day rather than the periods of darkness and light themselves; the pair functions as a merism for a complete day-cycle. The ordinal שְׁלִישִׁי is built from the root of שָׁלֹשׁ, "three." Note the pattern across the chapter: days one through five carry ordinals without the article (day one uses the cardinal אֶחָד, "one"), while the sixth and seventh days take the article, a subtle grammatical signal that the series is moving toward its climax. The closing פ in the Hebrew text is a scribal mark (petuḥah) indicating an open paragraph break.

Because the day-formula places evening before morning, later Jewish practice reckoned the calendar day from sunset to sunset, and Sabbath and festival observance follows this pattern to the present day. The ordered march of numbered days also stands in deliberate contrast to the cyclical, conflict-driven creation stories of Israel's neighbors, where the world emerges from struggle among deities rather than from an unhurried, measured sequence of divine speech.

The third day is the only day whose work receives the approval "it was good" twice (at the gathering of the waters and again at the appearance of vegetation), which is why no further evaluation appears in this closing verse. Readers have long debated whether these days denote ordinary solar days, a literary framework of six panels arranged in two parallel triads (days 1–3 forming realms, days 4–6 filling them), or extended ages; the repeated refrain itself makes no claim beyond marking completed stages, and the sun is not yet set in place until the following day.

text: And God said, "Let there be lights in the vault of the heavens to separate the day from the night, and let them be for signs and for seasons, for days and years,

versions.text: And God said, "Let there be lights in the vault of the heavens to separate day from night, and let them serve as signs to mark the seasons, the days, and the years,
versions.explanation: The Hebrew lists four coordinate items governed by the same preposition (for signs, and for seasons, and for days and years). Rendering it as "signs to mark the seasons, the days, and the years" subordinates the last three to "signs," an interpretive narrowing. The revision keeps the coordinate structure while reading smoothly aloud, and "separate the day from the night" matches the article in the Hebrew and balances the rhythm of the clause.

versions.text: And God said, "Let there be lights in the vault of the heavens to separate the day from the night, and let them serve as signs for seasons and for days and years,
versions.explanation: "serve as signs for seasons" still reads as though the seasons are what the signs mark, reintroducing the very subordination the coordinate Hebrew list avoids. "Let them be for signs and for seasons, for days and years" keeps each item on the same level, mirrors the repeated preposition, and echoes the parallel "and let them be lights" of the next verse, which aids oral flow.

footnotes.text: The Hebrew מְאֹרֹת (me'orot) is not the same word as the "light" (אוֹר) called into being on day one; it denotes light-bearers or luminaries — the same term used for the lamps of the sanctuary lampstand. "Lights" is chosen here for its plainness and rhythm; "luminaries" or "lamps" would be more precise but heavier on the tongue. רָקִיעַ is rendered "vault" (rather than the traditional "firmament" or the flatter "expanse") to preserve the image of an arched, solid-seeming dome over the earth. וּלְמוֹעֲדִים is given as "for seasons": the Hebrew means fixed, appointed times, and in later usage the sacred festivals; "seasons" is kept for its familiar cadence, though "appointed times" or "festivals" is the sharper sense. The verse ends with a comma because verses 14 and 15 are a single sentence in Hebrew — God's speech runs on and closes only in the next line.

מְאֹרֹת comes from the root אור, "to be light," with the prefix mem that commonly forms nouns of instrument or place — hence "light-holder," a lamp rather than radiance itself. The verb לְהַבְדִּיל, "to separate," is the same word used in verses 4, 6 and 7, binding the days of creation together as a work of ordering and dividing. Note the four-fold rhythm of the closing phrase — signs, appointed times, days, years — where the last item alone lacks the repeated preposition, a small quickening at the end of the list. The word מוֹעֵד is the root behind אֹהֶל מוֹעֵד, the "tent of meeting": an appointment in time or place.

The lights are given a function, not a personality. Sun and moon are not named here — nor in verse 16, where they appear only as "the greater light" and "the lesser light" — and many read this as deliberate restraint over against the surrounding cultures, where the heavenly bodies were themselves gods and the arbiters of fate. Here they are lamps hung in a vault, servants of time-keeping and of the earth beneath them. That they mark "signs" has been read in two directions: as the ordinary signals of calendar and weather, or as the occasional portents of Scripture's later prophecy. The reading that makes them oracles of individual destiny finds no footing in the text.

Israel's calendar was lunar-solar: months began with the sighting of the new moon, while the pilgrimage festivals were tied to the agricultural year, so both lights were needed to keep the reckoning straight. Ancient Mesopotamian and Egyptian astronomy was highly developed and inseparable from religion; celestial omen literature filled whole libraries. Against that background the sober functionalism of this verse — lights for dividing, for signs, for days and years — is striking.

The Greek tradition expands this verse, adding a phrase about giving light upon the earth already here in anticipation of the next verse, and it also reads "for signs and for appointed times and for days and for years" with the preposition repeated throughout. The Samaritan tradition spells מאורת in the fuller form found in verse 15. None of these variants alters the sense.

This verse is the classic warrant for the sanctification of the new moon and the fixing of the festival calendar in Jewish practice, and it echoes in the blessing over the moon and in Psalm 104:19, "He made the moon for appointed times." In Christian usage the verse belongs to the readings for the Easter Vigil and stands behind the ancient computations of the date of Easter.

text: and let them be lights in the vault of the heavens to shine on the earth." And it was so.

footnotes.text: The verse completes the divine command begun in verse 14, so the closing quotation mark falls after "earth." The Hebrew verb וְהָיוּ ("and they shall be") is a perfect with prefixed waw carrying forward the jussive force of "let there be" in the previous verse; hence "and let them be" rather than a flat future "and they will be." Some renderings prefer "let them serve as lights" or "let them be luminaries," which brings out the functional sense of the noun, but "lights" keeps the natural echo with "Let there be light" in verse 3 and with "the two great lights" in verse 16. "Vault" translates רָקִיעַ consistently with verses 6–8; "expanse" and "firmament" are common alternatives. The closing formula וַיְהִי־כֵן, "And it was so," is kept as a short, separate sentence, matching its use elsewhere in the chapter and giving the reader a natural pause before the narrative of verse 16.

The noun מָאוֹר (plural מְאוֹרֹת) is formed from the root אור, "to be light," with the prefix m- that typically marks an instrument or place: thus "light-bearer, lamp, luminary" rather than light itself. The same word designates the oil for the lamps of the sanctuary lampstand. Note the spelling: this verse writes מְאוֹרֹת fully, while verses 14 and 16 use shorter forms of the same word. The infinitive לְהָאִיר is a causative (hiphil) form, "to cause light to shine, to give light." רָקִיעַ derives from רקע, "to beat out, hammer flat," evoking something spread out like a sheet of beaten metal.

The luminaries are given a purely functional role: they mark time (v. 14) and illuminate the earth (v. 15). They are creatures with an assigned task, not powers to be feared or worshipped. This restraint is deliberate; even the words "sun" and "moon" are avoided in favour of "greater light" and "lesser light" in verse 16. Many readers also note the ordering of the account: light appears on the first day, its bearers only on the fourth, so that light is presented as God's gift rather than a property of the heavenly bodies themselves. "And it was so" underscores that the divine word alone is effective; the account of the making in verse 16 describes what the word has already accomplished.

In the surrounding cultures of the ancient Near East the sun and moon were major deities—Shamash and Sin in Mesopotamia, comparable figures in Egypt and Canaan—receiving temples, offerings and prayers, and consulted for omens. Against that background the language here is strikingly demythologizing. The heavenly bodies also governed the practical calendar: agricultural cycles, the lunar month, and the dating of festivals all depended on observing them, which explains why "signs, seasons, days and years" precede the mention of illumination.

The Hebrew tradition preserves both fuller and shorter spellings of the word for "lights" within these three verses, a common feature of Hebrew orthography that carries no difference in meaning. Ancient versions render the term with a word meaning "luminaries" or "light-givers." Some early witnesses expand the creation account at various points by repeating the command as a fulfilment report; the wording adopted here follows the traditional Hebrew text.

This passage belongs to the opening creation reading used in vigils and festal services of many Christian traditions, especially at the great Easter Vigil, where the sequence of light and lights sets the theme for the celebration. In Jewish daily prayer the morning blessing over light draws on the vocabulary of these verses in praising the God who forms light and creates the luminaries.

text: God made the two great lights—the greater light to govern the day and the lesser light to govern the night—and he made the stars.

footnotes.text: The Hebrew has two nouns in a row—"the great light for the dominion of the day"—with no verb repeated. Since Hebrew adjectives have no comparative form, the positive forms gadol ("great") and qaton ("small") are used comparatively here, so "greater" and "lesser" render the sense: of the two lights, one is the larger and one the smaller. The abstract noun memshelet ("dominion, rulership") has been turned into the verb "to govern" for smoother speech; a more literal rendering would be "for the dominion of the day … for the dominion of the night." The final clause is simply "and the stars," a third object of the opening verb; "and he made the stars" repeats the verb so that the sentence can be heard clearly when read aloud, after the long dash-set middle. The dashes reflect the structure of the Hebrew, where the two lights are named as an appositional unpacking of "the two great lights."

The noun ma'or is formed from the root 'or, "light," with a prefixed m- that often marks an instrument or place—hence "light-bearer, lamp, luminary" rather than light itself. The same word is used of the lamps of the sanctuary lampstand, which colors the picture here: the sky is furnished with lamps. The verb in this verse is 'asah, "make, fashion," not bara', "create," as in verse 1. Memshelet is the construct form of memshalah, from the root mashal, "to rule"; it denotes an exercised authority or realm of rule. Notably the ordinary Hebrew words for sun (shemesh) and moon (yareach) are avoided throughout the passage.

The avoidance of the names "sun" and "moon" is widely read as deliberate: in the surrounding cultures these were divine names, and here they are reduced to manufactured lamps, servants set in place by God. Their "dominion" is delegated and bounded—rule over a stretch of time, not over human destinies—which stands against astral religion and astrology. Readers have long noticed that light already appears on the first day, before the luminaries on the fourth; some take the days as a literary ordering (days one to three form spaces, days four to six fill them), others as distinguishing light itself from the bodies that carry it. The stars, objects of awe and worship elsewhere, are added almost in passing, as a brief final phrase.

In Mesopotamia the sun (Shamash) and moon (Sin) were major deities with temples, priesthoods and elaborate cults, and the stars were consulted for omens; in Egypt the sun god held the central place in royal ideology. The moon governed the month and the festival calendar across the ancient Near East, which is why the smaller light is granted its own "dominion" rather than being treated as a lesser accessory. Ancient observers described the two as "great" from the standpoint of apparent size and brightness in the sky, not physical magnitude.

The consonantal Hebrew text of this verse is stable across the witnesses, with only spelling variation in the word for "lights." The ancient Greek translation renders "for the dominion" with a plural expression, "for rulings/beginnings," of the day and of the night, and this plural wording fed later discussion of the luminaries as markers of times and seasons.

text: God set them in the vault of the heavens to shine on the earth,

footnotes.text: The Hebrew verb here is literally "gave" (natan), but in this context it carries the sense of placing or appointing something in a position; "set" preserves both the physical placement and the note of assignment to a task. The rendering "vault of the heavens" keeps the same wording used earlier in the chapter, so the reader hears the repetition; alternatives include "expanse of the sky" or the traditional "firmament of heaven." The verse ends with a comma rather than a period because in Hebrew verses 17 and 18 form a single flowing sentence: the lights are set there "to shine... to govern... to separate." Read aloud, the line should lean forward into what follows. "To shine on the earth" translates a causative form that could also be rendered "to give light upon the earth."

Three infinitive phrases hang on the one main verb: "to shine," "to govern," "to separate" (the last two in the following verse). Each begins with the preposition le- prefixed to the infinitive, expressing purpose, and the accumulation gives the passage its steady, list-like cadence. The noun raqia is related to a verb meaning to hammer or beat something out flat, as a metalworker spreads thin sheet — hence the picture of a stretched-out dome rather than empty air. The word for "heavens" is grammatically plural in form, an old dual-like ending that Hebrew keeps even where a single sky is meant.

Sun, moon and stars are here objects that are handled and positioned, assigned duties by the one who made them. In the surrounding cultures these same bodies were divine beings with names, temples and worshippers, and the astral cycle governed human destiny. This account withholds their names entirely, calling them simply the greater and lesser light, and reduces them to lamps hung in a vault. To an ancient hearer that would have sounded startling, even polemical.

The verse presses a distinction between Creator and creation: what other traditions worshipped, this text describes as furniture in a house. The lights have real authority — they "govern" — but it is delegated authority, held on assignment and directed outward for the benefit of the earth. Readers have long drawn from this a pattern for all created rule: dominion exists to give light to others, not to be adored in itself. Some interpreters also note that the lights serve the earth rather than the reverse, one of several places where this account orders creation toward the ground where living creatures will dwell.

The wording of this verse is remarkably stable across the ancient witnesses; the Greek and Samaritan traditions agree with the Hebrew, the Greek using its usual word for a solid "firmament" to render raqia, which shaped the traditional English rendering for centuries.

text: to govern the day and the night, and to separate the light from the darkness. And God saw that it was good.

footnotes.text: The verse continues the chain of purpose clauses begun in verse 17 (Hebrew infinitives with the preposition *le-*: "to shine… to govern… to separate"), so the translation opens with "to govern," letting the sentence run on from the previous line rather than starting a new independent statement. The verb *limshol* is rendered "govern" instead of "rule" or "have dominion," partly for rhythm and partly because it echoes the related noun in verse 16 ("for governing the day / the night") — the same root binds the two verses together. Hebrew says literally "to divide between the light and between the darkness," repeating the word "between"; English idiom is served by "to separate the light from the darkness." The closing clause has no verb "to be" in Hebrew — literally "and God saw that good" — so "that it was good" supplies what English requires, matching the refrain used throughout the chapter.

*Mashal* ("govern, rule") is ordinarily used of kings, stewards, and overseers, not of natural forces; here it casts the sun and moon as appointed officials with a delegated task. *Lehavdil* ("to separate") is a causative (hiphil) form of *badal*, the same verb used in verse 4, where God himself separates light from darkness; the priestly vocabulary of "separating" recurs later for holy and common, clean and unclean. The Masoretic pointing of the word here (*ûlăhavdîl*, with a reduced vowel under the *lamed*) is an unusual vocalization of the expected *ûlehavdîl*.

By assigning the lights a job — governing and separating — the text makes them servants rather than sovereigns. They "govern" only in the sense that a steward governs a household on the owner's behalf; the separating of light from darkness that God performed directly on day one is now entrusted to created instruments. The refrain "God saw that it was good" pronounces the verdict over these bodies too: they are creatures, neither divine nor demonic, and their ordering of time is part of a world called good.

In the surrounding cultures the sun and moon were named gods — worshipped, petitioned, and consulted for omens — and the calendar was a sacred science tied to their cults. This account never names them, calling them only the greater and lesser light, and describes them as timekeepers under appointment. For an audience familiar with astral religion and celestial divination, the language of delegated governance would have sounded like a deliberate demotion of the heavenly bodies.

The Samaritan tradition and some witnesses read the more regular spelling of "and to separate." Ancient translations render the verse without significant variation, and the closing refrain is uniformly attested, though some Greek witnesses expand it to "and God saw that they were good."

The fourth day belongs to the creation narrative read at vigils and festivals of creation, and its language of lights that govern day and night has long shaped evening and morning prayer, where the turning of light and darkness is received as an ordered gift rather than a contest of powers.

text: And there was evening, and there was morning—the fourth day.

footnotes.text: The refrain is rendered with the same wording used on the other creation days, since the Hebrew repeats itself word for word; keeping it identical lets the hearer feel the cadence of the week. The verbs are literally "and there was evening and there was morning" — the same verb hayah that runs through the chapter ("let there be… and there was"). The em dash stands in for a Hebrew construction with no connecting word at all: the phrase "fourth day" is simply set alongside what precedes it, and the dash gives the reader a place to breathe before the closing beat. Note also that Hebrew has no article here — strictly "a fourth day" — but English idiom and the sequence of counted days make "the fourth day" the natural reading for the ear.

The noun 'erev (evening) is related to a root suggesting mixing or dusk-blending, and boqer (morning) to a root meaning to break open or split — the light breaking through. Whether or not the ancient hearer consciously felt those etymologies, the pair functions as a merism: evening plus morning stands for the whole span of a day. The ordinal revi'i is built from arba' (four). Days one through five are anarthrous in Hebrew ("day one," "a second day"), while the sixth and seventh days take the definite article — a small grammatical signal that the sequence is building toward a climax.

Because the day is bounded evening-to-morning rather than sunrise-to-sunset, the Hebrew reckoning of a day beginning at nightfall is embedded in the very rhythm of the chapter; this is why Sabbath and festivals still begin at sundown. The placement of sun, moon, and stars on this particular day mattered for calendar-keeping: the luminaries are given as markers for "appointed times." Some ancient Jewish groups, including the community behind certain Dead Sea texts, built a solar calendar in which the year began on the fourth day of the week, precisely because that is when the heavenly lights were set in place.

The closing refrain quietly makes a polemical point. In the surrounding cultures the sun and moon were deities whose movements ruled human fate; here they have just been made, assigned a task, pronounced good, and folded into an ordinary working day that ends like all the others. The measured repetition also presents time itself as God's creature — ordered, bounded, and rhythmic — which becomes the ground for the Sabbath pattern that the chapter is moving toward.

The Masoretic text closes the verse with a petuchah (פ), a scribal marker indicating an open paragraph break before the fifth day; such markers are part of the received layout rather than the wording, and some manuscripts differ slightly in the type of break used. The ancient Greek and Samaritan traditions agree with the Hebrew wording of the refrain here; no substantive variants affect the sense.

This refrain has long served as a natural stopping point in public reading of the creation account, and the six-fold repetition has shaped liturgical practice: creation narratives read at vigils are often divided at these very lines, with a sung response or a moment of silence after each day. The evening-then-morning order also underlies the daily office pattern in which the liturgical day opens with evening prayer.

text: And God said, "Let the waters teem with swarms of living creatures, and let birds fly above the earth across the face of the vault of the heavens."

versions.text: And God said, "Let the waters swarm with living creatures, and let birds fly above the earth across the vault of the heavens."
versions.explanation: The Hebrew has a cognate accusative (יִשְׁרְצוּ ... שֶׁרֶץ), which the current rendering flattens; 'teem with swarms of living creatures' preserves the doubled force without the awkward 'swarm with swarms.' Also restores 'the face of' (עַל־פְּנֵי), which adds the expansive image and improves the closing rhythm for oral reading.

footnotes.text: The Hebrew builds two verbs on their own nouns: literally "let the waters swarm swarms of living soul" and "let bird fly about." English cannot easily double a word this way without sounding clumsy, so the rendering keeps the effect with "teem with swarms," preserving the sense of restless multiplication while staying readable aloud. "Living creatures" translates the singular collective *nefesh ḥayyah*, often rendered "living soul" or "living being"; here it means simply animate life, not a spiritual faculty. "Birds" renders a collective singular ("bird," i.e., flying things as a class), and the plural is used for natural English. The last phrase is literally "upon the face of the expanse of the heavens": the birds move across the underside of the dome, not within it, and "vault" is chosen for the same word rendered elsewhere as "expanse" or "firmament," a stretched or hammered-out canopy. Some read the phrase as "in the open expanse of the sky," a smoother but less literal option.

*šereṣ* and the verb *šāraṣ* describe small creatures that move in dense, wriggling masses; the same root later covers swarming things on land. The verb *yeʿofēp* is an intensive (polel) form of "fly," suggesting continuous flitting or hovering rather than a single flight. Both clauses use a cognate accusative — verb and object from one root — a favorite Hebrew device for intensity, giving the line an audible rhythm: *yišrəṣû... šereṣ*, *ʿôp yeʿôpēp*. *rāqîaʿ* derives from a root meaning to beat or hammer out thin, as metal is spread into a sheet.

Unlike the third and sixth days, the waters are not told to bring forth by their own power; the command is simply that life appear, and the next verse states that God himself created it. Life in sea and sky is therefore a direct divine work, not a property of the elements. Ancient neighbors told of sea monsters and sky powers as rival deities; here they are creatures summoned by a word. Readers have also noticed that the blessing of fertility (v. 22) falls first on these creatures, linking abundance in the sea and air with God's generosity rather than with any struggle among gods.

The verse reflects a widely shared ancient picture of the world: a solid dome holding back the upper waters, with birds moving in the open air just beneath it. Sea and sky were the two realms least under human control, and in surrounding cultures they were populated by feared powers. Fish and waterfowl were also everyday food and imagery for peoples living near the Nile, the Mediterranean, and the great rivers, so the abundance described here would have sounded like plenty as much as like cosmology.

Several early witnesses, including the main Greek tradition, add "and it was so" at the end of this verse, matching the pattern of the other creative commands. The traditional Hebrew text does not have it, and most editions follow the shorter reading, since the fulfillment is spelled out in the following verse.

text: So God created the great sea creatures and every living creature that moves, with which the waters teemed, according to their kinds, and every winged bird according to its kind. And God saw that it was good.

versions.text: So God created the great sea creatures and every living thing that moves, with which the waters swarm, according to their kinds, and every winged bird according to its kind. And God saw that it was good.
versions.explanation: Two small consistency/flow refinements: 'nephesh chayyah' was rendered 'living creatures' in verse 20, so 'living creature' here keeps the vocabulary consistent and better reflects the phrase than the vaguer 'living thing'; and 'teem' echoes the verb used in verse 20 for the same root, tightening the link between God's command and its fulfillment. The rhythm of the clause also reads more smoothly aloud.

versions.text: So God created the great sea creatures and every living creature that moves, with which the waters teem, according to their kinds, and every winged bird according to its kind. And God saw that it was good.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew verb שָׁרְצוּ is a perfect, describing the completed creative act of the sixth-day narrative rather than an ongoing state; the past tense 'teemed' matches the surrounding narrative sequence ('created... saw') and keeps the echo with the command of v. 20 while reading naturally aloud. This is a minor refinement only; the present-tense rendering is defensible.

footnotes.text: The opening verb is rendered "So God created" rather than simply "And God created": the connective marks this act as the fulfillment of the command spoken in the previous verse. The verb here is the same one used in verse 1 and again for humanity in verse 27 — one of only three occurrences in the chapter — and English "created" preserves that deliberate repetition rather than varying it with "made" or "formed." "Great sea creatures" translates a term whose range runs from "sea monsters" and "dragons" to "serpents" and "crocodiles"; older renderings offered "whales." The neutral "sea creatures" avoids importing mythological color that the Hebrew text itself deliberately downplays, while "great" retains the sense of vast, awe-inspiring size. The clause "with which the waters teem" keeps the verbal link to verse 20 ("let the waters teem"), where the same root appears; a more literal rendering would be "which the waters swarmed forth," and some prefer "that the waters brought forth in swarms." "Every winged bird" reflects a Hebrew phrase that literally reads "every bird of wing."

The word rendered "teem" (root š-r-ṣ) is used in a striking way: the waters are the grammatical subject of a transitive verb, so the sense is that the waters swarmed the creatures forth. The related noun in verse 20 ("swarms") comes from the same root, producing a cognate construction — literally "let the waters swarm a swarm" — a sound-play that this verse echoes. The participle translated "that moves" (rōmeśet) describes gliding, creeping, or scurrying motion and is feminine singular, agreeing with the collective "living creature" (nepeš ḥayyâ, literally "breathing being" or "living soul"). Note also the shift in the phrase "according to their kinds": it is plural for the water creatures (many species) but singular in "according to its kind" for the birds, a variation the translation preserves.

In the surrounding cultures the great sea dragon was a primeval adversary — a chaos monster defeated by a warrior deity before the world could be ordered. Here the sea creatures are neither rivals nor pre-existing powers: they are simply creatures, made by God on the same day as the fish and birds, and pronounced good along with everything else. The choice of the verb "created" (reserved in this chapter for the cosmos itself, the great sea creatures, and humankind) may signal precisely this polemical point — even the most fearsome beings imaginable owe their existence to God's word. Elsewhere in Scripture these same creatures are summoned to praise their Maker, and the divine "good" pronounced here extends the goodness of creation to what human beings find most alien and terrifying.

Ancient Near Eastern art and literature depicted the sea as the realm of monstrous serpents and dragons, and seafaring peoples told of vast beasts encountered beyond the coastal waters. The Hebrew term used here also names ordinary large reptiles — crocodiles of the Nile, for example, are called by this word in prophetic imagery. For a largely land-based, non-seafaring people, the deep waters were a place of danger and mystery, which makes the calm listing of its inhabitants among God's ordered handiwork all the more pointed.

The word for the sea creatures appears in the traditional consonantal text in a shortened spelling, which some later manuscripts and versions write out more fully; the meaning is unaffected. Ancient translations render the phrase as "the great sea monsters" or "the great whales." Some witnesses add a conjunction or vary the wording of the relative clause about the waters, but no variant changes the substance of the verse.

text: God blessed them and said, "Be fruitful and multiply and fill the waters of the seas, and let the birds multiply on the earth."

footnotes.text: The Hebrew reads literally "And God blessed them, saying," with the infinitive לֵאמֹר (le'mor) functioning as a quotation marker rather than a separate act of speech. Rendering it "God blessed them and said" keeps the line short and speakable, since "saying" before direct speech sounds stilted in English. The phrase אֶת־הַמַּיִם בַּיַּמִּים is literally "the waters in the seas"; "the waters of the seas" preserves the sense while avoiding the double preposition that clogs the mouth when read aloud. The final clause shifts from second-person command to third-person wish — literally "and let the bird become many in the land" — so "let the birds multiply" reproduces the change of grammatical person; the collective singular הָעוֹף ("bird, fowl") is rendered as an English plural, as in the previous verse. Some render the last verb as a simple future, "and the birds will multiply," but the jussive form favors the volitional sense of a blessing being pronounced.

The pairing פְּרוּ וּרְבוּ (peru urevu) is a rhyming imperative pair — "bear fruit and become many" — where פרה evokes the fruiting of a tree or vine applied to animal and human offspring. There is deliberate sound-play between הַמַּיִם (ha-mayim, "the waters") and בַּיַּמִּים (ba-yammim, "in the seas"), two words built on nearly the same consonants; the ear hears the waters filling the seas before the mind parses it. The verb יִרֶב is the shortened (apocopated) jussive of רבה, the same root as וּרְבוּ, so the birds' increase is expressed with the identical verb used for the sea creatures, binding the two halves of the blessing together.

This is the first blessing spoken in Scripture, and it is spoken over animals, not over humans. Blessing here is not merely a kind word but an empowering gift: the capacity to reproduce and to fill space is conferred by God rather than possessed inherently. The same words are addressed to humanity in verse 28, with the added charge to subdue and rule, and they are renewed to Noah and his sons after the flood — a signal that the creation blessing survives judgment.
