Notably the creatures said to be blessed include the great sea creatures of the previous verse, which elsewhere in the ancient world were figures of chaos to be defeated; here they are simply creatures under blessing. Some interpreters ask why the birds are addressed in the third person rather than directly; suggestions range from stylistic variation to a distinction between the waters, which are commanded to teem, and the dry land, which has not yet been filled.

In the surrounding cultures of the ancient Near East, fertility of flocks, fish, and fields was typically secured through cultic appeasement of deities associated with storm, sea, and grain. Here abundance is not negotiated but granted once and for all by a single God at the outset, embedded in the structure of creation itself. "The seas" in the plural reflects a worldview in which the waters are a vast, undifferentiated realm, while birds are located "on the earth" rather than in the heavens — consistent with verse 20, where they fly across the face of the expanse but belong among the creatures of the land.

The verse is textually stable across the major witnesses. Ancient translations render the final clause with a plural verb for the birds, smoothing the collective singular of the Hebrew, but this reflects the target languages rather than a different underlying text. The Masoretic accentuation places a major pause after לֵאמֹר, marking the transition from narration to the divine speech.

As part of the fifth-day reading, this verse belongs to the creation account used in vigil services and in seasonal celebrations of creation. The words "be fruitful and multiply" have long been echoed in marriage rites and in prayers of thanksgiving for harvest, birth, and the blessing of animals.

text: And there was evening, and there was morning—the fifth day.

footnotes.text: The refrain is rendered with the same wording used on the other creation days, preserving the formula's repetitive, chant-like quality that is essential for oral reading. The dash before "the fifth day" reflects the Hebrew, which simply juxtaposes the noun phrase without a verb or conjunction; alternatives such as "a fifth day" or "that was the fifth day" are possible, but the dash keeps the terse cadence of the original while signaling the summarizing force of the phrase. Hebrew 'erev and boqer are translated "evening" and "morning" rather than "dusk" and "dawn," keeping the ordinary, unhurried vocabulary of the refrain.

The Hebrew wayehi-'erev wayehi-voqer uses the narrative verb form of hayah ("to be, become, come to pass") twice, an economical construction that could be heard either as "there was evening, there was morning" or "evening came, and morning came." The ordinal ḥamishi ("fifth") is built on the numeral ḥamesh, "five." Unlike days one through five, which lack the definite article in most of the sequence, the sixth day takes the article, marking a subtle progression toward completion. The verse ends with the scribal marker peh, indicating an open paragraph break in the Hebrew manuscripts.

The order "evening... morning" has long been read as the basis for reckoning the day from sunset to sunset, a practice reflected in later Israelite worship and sabbath observance. Others read the phrase as marking the close of the day's work rather than defining when a day begins: darkness falls, dawn returns, and the completed day is named. Either way, the refrain frames creation as ordered, measured time rather than timeless myth.

The fifth day concludes the work of filling the sea and sky, corresponding to the second day's separation of waters and heavens. This symmetry between days one through three (forming realms) and days four through six (filling them) shapes the whole account, and the recurring refrain functions as the seam that joins each panel to the next.

The refrain of the creation days is read in synagogue and church at the opening of the annual cycle of Torah readings and in vigil services celebrating creation, where its measured repetition invites responsive or antiphonal reading.

text: And God said, "Let the earth bring forth living creatures according to their kinds: livestock, creeping things, and wild animals of the earth, each according to its kind." And it was so.

versions.text: And God said, "Let the land bring forth living creatures according to their kinds: livestock, creeping things, and wild animals, each according to its kind." And it was so.
versions.explanation: הָאָרֶץ is rendered "earth" elsewhere in the chapter (vv. 1, 10, 11, 12); "land" breaks that consistency and weakens the echo of "let the earth sprout." Also, וְחַיְתוֹ־אֶרֶץ is literally "wild animals of the earth"; including "of the earth" preserves the phrase and gives the clause a fuller cadence for reading aloud, while still matching v. 25's "wild animals."

footnotes.text: The Hebrew phrase nephesh chayyah is grammatically singular but functions as a collective, so it is rendered as the plural "living creatures." Older renderings such as "living soul" or "living thing" are possible, but the expression denotes animate, breathing life rather than an immaterial soul. The three groups are named with terms whose ranges overlap: behemah covers domesticated herd animals ("livestock" or "cattle"), remes covers small creatures that move low along the ground ("creeping things," including reptiles and insects), and chayyat erets covers undomesticated "wild animals" or "beasts of the earth." The phrase "according to their kinds" is repeated in the Hebrew, and the repetition is kept because it carries the rhythm of the verse; the second occurrence is given as "each according to its kind" so that the line does not sound merely redundant when read aloud. The closing "And it was so" translates a short Hebrew clause (wayhi khen) that recurs as a refrain through the chapter and is kept short here for the same cadence.

"Let the earth bring forth" renders a causative (hiphil) verb form used as a command directed at the land itself, parallel to the waters being told to swarm with life in verse 20. The word for "wild animals" appears in the archaic form chayto-erets, with an unusual ending on the construct noun that is otherwise found chiefly in poetry — a small trace of older poetic diction inside the prose account. The possessive suffix on "its kind" is feminine singular and can refer back either to the collective "living creature" or to "the earth," which is why translations differ between "their kinds" and "its kind." The noun remes is built from a verb meaning to move or glide along, describing manner of movement rather than a zoological class.

The land animals share with human beings both the sixth day and the designation nephesh chayyah, "living creature" — the same phrase later applied to humanity. This places animals and people in one shared category of breathing, earth-bound life, even as the following verses set humanity apart by image and vocation. God's speaking to the earth so that it brings forth life has long been read as creation working through mediating means rather than by immediate fiat alone. The recurring "according to their kinds" has been taken by some as a statement about fixed boundaries in the created order, and by others as a description of the ordered variety and fruitfulness of life rather than a claim about biological mechanism.

The threefold grouping reflects how an agrarian community actually encountered animal life: the herds it kept and depended on, the game and predators beyond the settlement, and the small creatures that moved through field, house, and soil. Such practical classification also stands behind the later dietary distinctions in Israelite law. In the surrounding creation stories of the ancient Near East, animals frequently originate from the bodies or offspring of gods; here they are simply brought forth from the ground at a word, and the earth is a creature, not a deity.

The early Greek tradition renders behemah as "four-footed animals" and lists the three groups in a different order, beginning with the four-footed beasts; some witnesses of that tradition also anticipate wording from the following verse. These are stylistic and harmonizing adjustments rather than evidence of a different Hebrew text, which is stable here.

This verse belongs to the opening creation reading used at vigils and at seasons celebrating God as maker of all things, and its refrain of living creatures brought forth from the earth has furnished language for hymns and canticles that call all creation to praise.

text: And God made the wild animals according to their kinds, the livestock according to their kinds, and everything that creeps along the ground according to its kind. And God saw that it was good.

versions.text: God made the wild animals according to their kinds, the livestock according to their kinds, and everything that creeps along the ground according to its kind. And God saw that it was good.
versions.explanation: The surrounding verses render the waw-consecutive chain with a connective ("And God said...", "Then God said..."). Beginning this verse with "And God made" preserves the narrative rhythm of the creation account and reads more naturally aloud in sequence with verse 24.

footnotes.text: Hebrew uses collective singulars here: "the living thing of the earth" (chayyat ha'arets) and "the cattle" (ha-behemah) each stand for a whole class of creature, so English plurals — "the wild animals," "the livestock" — carry the sense more naturally. The possessive suffix on l'minah is likewise singular ("according to its kind"), but it is matched here to the English plural nouns as "according to their kinds"; the third phrase keeps the singular "according to its kind" because "everything that creeps" is grammatically singular in English, exactly mirroring the Hebrew shift to l'minehu. The triple refrain "according to ... kind(s)" is deliberately preserved rather than trimmed, since the repetition is the audible backbone of the verse when read aloud. The closing clause has no expressed object in Hebrew ("and God saw that good"); "that it was good" supplies the natural English copula, and could equally be rendered "how good it was."

The verb here is 'asah, "to make, fashion," not bara', "to create," which appeared for the heavens and earth and returns for the great sea creatures and for humanity. Hebrew narrative uses the two verbs as poetic partners rather than strict technical terms. Note also the switch of nouns: verse 24 speaks of the creeping things of ha'arets ("the earth, land"), while this verse says remes ha'adamah, "the creeping things of the soil, the tilled ground." 'Adamah is the dust-word from which 'adam ("human") is drawn in the following verses, quietly linking the small ground-dwellers with the creature about to be formed from the same soil. The word min, "kind," is used in the Hebrew Bible chiefly of animals and plants in classification lists; it denotes an observable, reproducing category rather than a term of formal biological taxonomy.

Verse 24 has God summon the animals out of the earth; verse 25 says God himself made them. The two statements together guard a careful balance: the earth is genuinely fruitful, yet the animals are not offspring of the soil or of any lesser power — God is their direct maker. The threefold "according to its kind" affirms an ordered, differentiated world rather than an undivided mass, and the verdict "good" pronounces the animal world valuable in itself, before any human being exists to use it. Unlike the sea creatures and birds of the fifth day, the land animals receive no blessing of fruitfulness here; many readers see this as leaving room for the blessing that will be spoken over humanity, made on the same sixth day.

The three categories — domesticated herd animals, wild game, and small creatures that swarm close to the ground — reflect the way ancient Near Eastern peoples actually sorted the animal world, by relationship to human settlement rather than by anatomy. Order matters in the telling: in the announcement of verse 24 livestock came first, while in the fulfilment here the wild animals lead, a common Hebrew way of varying a repeated list. In neighbouring creation stories animals could be born of gods or embody divine powers; here bulls, serpents and lions alike are simply creatures, made and appraised by God.

The traditional Hebrew text ends verse 24 with "and it was so" and closes verse 25 with the verdict of goodness. Some ancient witnesses arrange the formulas differently, placing "and it was so" after the account of the making rather than after the command, a harmonizing pattern found elsewhere in the chapter. Certain versions also smooth the list by reading "creeping things of the earth" here instead of "of the ground," matching the previous verse. The reading translated follows the received Hebrew text with its deliberate variation.

text: Then God said, "Let us make man in our image, according to our likeness, and let them rule over the fish of the sea and the birds of the sky, over the livestock and all the earth, and over every creature that creeps along the ground."

footnotes.text: The Hebrew 'adam is rendered "man" in the collective sense of humankind, not as a personal name or as a reference to males alone; the following verse makes this explicit with "male and female." The shift from singular "man" to plural "let them rule" mirrors the Hebrew exactly, where a singular collective noun takes a plural verb. "In our image, according to our likeness" preserves the two different Hebrew prepositions (be- and ke-); some render both as "in," but the variation is audible in the original and worth keeping. The verb translated "rule" (radah) is a strong term of dominion; "have dominion" is a common alternative, but "rule" reads more naturally aloud. "Birds of the sky" translates a phrase literally meaning "flyer of the heavens," and "creature that creeps along the ground" keeps the same wording used in the preceding verses for consistency.

Tselem ("image") elsewhere denotes a carved statue or representation, while demut ("likeness") is a more abstract term for resemblance. Their pairing here is likely a form of poetic reinforcement rather than a distinction between two separate qualities. The phrase "every creature that creeps" (kol-haremes haromes) is a figura etymologica, a noun and participle from the same root stacked together for emphasis — something like "every creeper that creeps." The verb na'aseh ("let us make") is a cohortative, the form used for self-encouragement or shared resolve.

The plural "let us make" has been read in several ways: as a plural of majesty or deliberation, as God addressing the heavenly court of angelic beings, as divine self-address, or, in much Christian reading, as an early intimation of plurality within the Godhead. The immediately following verse reverts to singular verbs ("he created"), which cautions against pressing the plural too far. The image of God (imago Dei) has carried enormous doctrinal weight: it has been located in reason, in moral capacity, in relational personhood, and in the human vocation to represent God on earth. The mandate to "rule" has likewise been debated — whether it licenses exploitation or entrusts humanity with stewardship on behalf of the Creator, a reading supported by the royal-representative sense of image language.

In the wider ancient Near East, kings and occasionally priests were described as the image or likeness of a god — living representatives of the deity's rule in a particular territory. Statues of a king set up in outlying provinces functioned as visible signs of his authority. Against that background, the claim that all humanity bears the divine image is striking: a royal dignity normally reserved for the monarch is extended to every human being.

The Hebrew reads "and over all the earth," which sits oddly in a list otherwise made up of living creatures. Some ancient versions read instead "and over all the wild animals of the earth," a wording that would match the animal catalogue of verses 24-25 and differs by only one word in Hebrew. The traditional Hebrew reading is retained here, since the broader phrase also fits the sweeping scope of the dominion granted.

This verse has long anchored liturgies of creation and of human dignity. Genesis 1 is read at vigils marking new beginnings and at festivals celebrating the completion and renewal of the Scripture reading cycle, and this verse in particular is frequently cited in marriage rites, in prayers at the beginning of life, and in funeral liturgies affirming the worth of the person.

text: So God created man in his own image; in the image of God he created him; male and female he created them.

footnotes.text: The Hebrew has the definite article, hā'ādām, "the man" — a collective term for humanity rather than a personal name. "Man" is retained here because it preserves the link with the preceding verse ("Let us make man") and because it matches the singular pronoun "him" that follows; alternatives such as "humankind," "humanity," or "human beings" convey the inclusive sense more directly but break the singular-to-plural movement of the Hebrew. The verse is laid out as three short lines, and the translation keeps that shape with semicolons and repeated "he created," so that the threefold hammering of the verb can be heard when read aloud. The phrase "in his own image" renders bətsalmô, where "own" is not a separate Hebrew word but marks the possessive suffix clearly for the ear.

The verb bārā' ("create") occurs three times in this one verse; in the Hebrew Bible it takes only God as its subject and never names a material worked upon, which sets divine creating apart from ordinary making ('āśāh, used in v. 26). Tselem, "image," elsewhere denotes a carved statue or representation, even an idol (compare its use for cast figures); demût in v. 26, "likeness," softens or explains it. Zākār ûneqēbāh, "male and female," are the plain biological terms also applied to animals (as in the flood narrative), not the relational words "man and woman" ('îš and 'iššāh) that appear in chapter 2. The vertical stroke (paseq) after "God" in the Hebrew text marks a slight pause, giving the reading a measured, solemn cadence.

This verse is the classic ground of the doctrine that human beings bear the image of God (imago Dei). Interpreters have located the image variously in reason and spiritual capacity, in moral likeness, in the mandate to rule as God's representatives on earth, and in human relationality — the last often supported by the shift from "him" to "them." The text itself does not define the image; it simply asserts it, and grounds on it the dignity of every human life (compare the reason given for prohibiting bloodshed later in Genesis). The movement from singular "him" to plural "them" has been read as showing that the image belongs to humanity as a whole and equally to male and female, neither sex possessing it more fully than the other. That God is described in male-and-female humanity's creation does not imply sexuality in God; rather, human sexual differentiation is presented as part of the good created order and as the basis for the blessing of fruitfulness in the next verse.

In the surrounding cultures of the ancient Near East, the language of "image" belonged chiefly to kings and to cult statues: an Egyptian pharaoh could be called the living image of a god, and a royal statue erected in a distant province represented the absent ruler's authority. Genesis takes this royal and cultic vocabulary and democratizes it, applying it to every human being, male and female alike. This is striking in a book that elsewhere forbids making images of God: humanity itself, not any crafted object, is God's representation in the world. It also stands in contrast to Mesopotamian creation accounts in which humans are fashioned to relieve the gods of labor and supply them with food.

The Hebrew text of this verse is stable across the witnesses. The early Greek tradition reads "and God made the man," using its ordinary verb for making rather than distinguishing it from "create," and some Greek copies omit or vary the first "in his own image" through the natural slip of repeated phrases; the Samaritan tradition and the ancient versions otherwise agree with the received Hebrew.

The verse belongs to the opening creation reading used in the great vigil of Easter and in many services of thanksgiving for creation. It is also among the most frequently read texts at marriage services, where "male and female he created them" is joined to Genesis 2, and it is widely cited in prayers and liturgies concerned with human dignity, justice, and the care of the vulnerable.

text: God blessed them and said to them, "Be fruitful and multiply; fill the earth and subdue it. Rule over the fish of the sea, the birds of the sky, and every living thing that moves on the earth."

footnotes.text: The five imperatives of the blessing — "Be fruitful and multiply; fill the earth and subdue it. Rule…" — render Hebrew plural commands addressed to both the man and the woman together. The rendering splits them into two sentences for oral rhythm: the first three verbs form a natural triad of increase, the last two a pair of dominion. "Subdue it" translates a strong verb often used of bringing land or enemies under control; softer options like "take charge of it" or "cultivate it" are possible but weaken the force of the Hebrew. "Rule over" (some render "have dominion") governs three prepositional phrases; the English repeats "the" rather than the Hebrew's repeated preposition, and adds "and" before the last item for a smooth spoken cadence. "The birds of the sky" could equally be "of the heavens," the same word rendered "heavens" in verse 1; "sky" is chosen here because the birds fly in the visible air. "Every living thing that moves" renders a phrase for creatures that creep or crawl along the ground.

The verbs *peru urevu* ("be fruitful and multiply") form an assonant pair that echoes through the book, repeated to the sea creatures and birds in verse 22 and later to Noah and to the patriarchs. *Kavash* ("subdue") elsewhere describes subjugating land, servants, or opponents — it presumes resistance. *Radah* ("rule") is used of a king's or master's governance and is deliberately distinct from the ordinary verb for "rule" applied within Israel's households. The wordplay between *radah* (rule) and *yarad* (go down) has attracted rabbinic comment: if humanity rules rightly it ascends, if not, it descends.

This verse is the charter of what is often called the creation mandate or cultural mandate. Because the commission follows immediately upon the statement that humanity bears God's image, the dominion granted is understood by most interpreters as a delegated, representative rule — humanity governs on God's behalf and answers to him, not as an owner with unlimited license. Read alongside the later charge to work and keep the garden, and in light of the strictly plant-based diet of the next verse, "subdue" and "rule" are widely taken to describe stewardship and cultivation rather than exploitation. Note also that the words are first a blessing, not merely a command: fertility, land, and authority are gifts before they are duties.

In the surrounding cultures of the ancient Near East, the "image" of a deity and royal dominion over the earth were normally the prerogative of the king alone; some accounts even describe humanity as created to relieve the gods of labour. Here the royal vocabulary of image and rule is extended to humankind as a whole, male and female alike, and their task is blessing rather than servitude. Filling and subduing the earth would have resonated with an agrarian audience for whom clearing, tilling, and settling untamed land was the work of generations.

The Hebrew text is stable here. In *vekhivshuha* ("and subdue it") the traditional consonantal text writes the word without the expected letter for the object suffix, while the reading tradition supplies the feminine singular "it" referring to the earth; ancient versions all reflect this reading. Some early Jewish commentators drew moral inferences from the defective spelling.

The verse is read in synagogue as part of the opening Torah portion and in many churches at the celebration of creation and at the Easter Vigil. Its blessing of fruitfulness has long been used in marriage liturgies, and it is frequently cited in prayers and services concerned with care for creation and human responsibility for the environment.

text: And God said, "Look, I have given you every seed-bearing plant on the face of all the earth and every tree that bears fruit with seed in it. They will be your food.

footnotes.text: The interjection הִנֵּה is rendered "Look" rather than the older "Behold" to keep the line speakable; it is a pointer that draws attention to what follows, and here it introduces a formal grant. The verb נָתַתִּי is a perfect, and can be read either as a simple past ("I have given") or as a so-called performative perfect, where the act happens in the speaking: "I hereby give you." Both senses are alive in the Hebrew, and "I have given" preserves the finished, settled quality of the gift. The Hebrew of the second half runs literally "every tree in which is fruit of a tree bearing seed"; the doubled "tree" is smoothed here to "every tree that bears fruit with seed in it." The closing clause is literally "to you it shall be for food" with a singular verb governing the whole collection; English needs the plural, so "They will be your food." Note that the sentence is left open at the end of the verse—the quotation continues and closes only in the next verse.

זֹרֵעַ זֶרַע is a figura etymologica, a participle paired with its own cognate noun—"seeding seed"—the same phrase used of the plants in verses 11–12, binding the food grant back to the third day of creation. עֵשֶׂב denotes low, seed-bearing vegetation (herbage, grain, garden plants) as distinct from דֶּשֶׁא, the fresh green growth of verse 11, and from עֵץ, woody trees. לְאָכְלָה is a noun with the preposition ל, "for eating, as food," not a verb; the same word governs the animals' portion in the next verse. The phrase עַל־פְּנֵי כָל־הָאָרֶץ, "on the face of all the earth," stresses that the gift is not local but as wide as the world.

The diet assigned here is entirely vegetarian: plants and fruit, for humans and animals alike. Permission to eat meat is granted only after the flood, and readers have long debated whether this points to an original peaceable order later conceded to human violence, or is simply the narrator's way of saying that God provides abundantly. Note also the theology of the verb: humanity has just been told to rule and subdue, but food is not taken by right—it is given. Dominion is exercised inside a gift. The plants are not described as having נֶפֶשׁ חַיָּה, "living breath," as the animals are, which is one reason later interpreters saw no violence in eating them.

In several older creation stories of the ancient Near East, humanity is made to labor for the gods and to keep them supplied with food. Here the pattern is reversed: the deity provides for the creatures. The two categories named, field crops and orchard fruit, mirror the actual agricultural economy of the region—grain and pulses from sown fields, and the produce of vine, fig, olive and other trees.

The Masoretic text places a paseq, a small vertical stroke, after עֵשֶׂב, a scribal mark separating words to guard the reading. Ancient versions render the doubled "fruit of a tree" in the second clause more smoothly than the Hebrew does, but there is no substantial variation in the sense of the verse.
The verse has long been read at harvest thanksgivings and is a common source for table graces and blessings over food, and in more recent practice for liturgies of creation care and stewardship.

text: And to every wild animal of the earth, every bird of the sky, and every creature that moves on the ground—everything that has life in it—I give every green plant for food." And it was so.

versions.text: And to every wild animal of the earth, every bird of the sky, and everything that moves on the ground—everything that has the breath of life—I give every green plant for food." And it was so.
versions.explanation: Two small refinements: (1) 'everything' occurs three times in close succession, which sounds clunky when read aloud; changing the first to 'every creature that moves' varies the rhythm. (2) The Hebrew here is 'nefesh chayyah' (a living being/life in it), not 'nishmat chayyim' (breath of life); 'everything that has life in it' renders the phrase more precisely while keeping the oral flow.

footnotes.text: Hebrew has no verb in this verse; it depends grammatically on "I have given" in verse 29, and reads literally: "and to every living thing of the earth... every green of plant for food." Because a verbless clause of that length is hard to follow when heard aloud, the translation supplies "I give," placing it after the long list of recipients so the sentence lands clearly. The dashes mark off the Hebrew relative clause "which has in it living breath," which describes all three groups of creatures, not just the last. The single Hebrew word for land/earth occurs three times here; it is rendered "earth" and then "ground" so the repetition does not become wearisome to the ear.

"Wild animal of the earth" translates a phrase built on the word for "living thing," the ordinary designation for undomesticated land animals; "bird of the sky" is literally "flyer of the heavens." The word rendered "creature that moves" is a participle meaning to creep, crawl, or swarm — used of small scurrying land animals, not only of reptiles. "Life in it" renders nephesh ḥayyah, literally "living breath" or "living being"; the same phrase is used of the human being in chapter 2, so it marks shared creaturely life rather than a distinct human soul. "Green plant" is literally "greenness of herbage," a collective phrase for all leafy growth.

Humans receive seeds and fruit (v. 29); animals receive the green foliage. Read straightforwardly, the original order of creation involves no killing for food — permission to eat meat comes only after the flood. Interpreters differ on how much weight to place on this: some read it as a picture of an original peaceable creation to be restored in the age of harmony promised by the prophets; others read it as a way of saying that God, not competition or chance, is the source of every creature's sustenance. Either way, the animals are not merely resources for humanity but recipients of divine provision in their own right, which shapes how human dominion in verse 28 should be understood.

The closing formula "and it was so" rounds off the creative speech of the sixth day, matching the pattern used on earlier days. Ancient versions likewise lack an explicit verb of giving in this verse; the Greek tradition adds a further phrase about creeping things and keeps the closing formula, while the Latin tradition supplies a purpose clause ("that they may have to feed on") to smooth the same grammatical gap that this translation resolves with "I give."

Genesis 1 is a foundational reading in vigils and festivals of creation, and verses 29-30 are frequently used in harvest thanksgivings, blessings over food, and services concerned with the care of animals and the land.

text: God saw all that he had made, and behold, it was very good. And there was evening, and there was morning—the sixth day.

versions.text: God saw all that he had made, and it was very good indeed. And there was evening, and there was morning—the sixth day.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew וְהִנֵּה adds a note of presentation ("and behold"), which the current "indeed" absorbs into the intensifier מְאֹד ("very"), producing the slightly redundant "very good indeed." Rendering הִנֵּה explicitly preserves the distinct force of both words and gives a cleaner cadence for oral reading, while keeping consistency with the repeated refrain of the chapter.

footnotes.text: The verse follows the Hebrew word order and its two-part rhythm: a survey of the whole work, then the closing day-formula. "Behold" renders the Hebrew particle *hinneh*, which invites the hearer to look with God at what he sees; more colloquial options ("and it was indeed very good," "look — it was very good") lose the pause that the particle creates in oral reading, so the traditional "behold" is kept. "All that he had made" translates *kol asher asah*, a summary of the whole six-day work rather than only the creatures of day six; the past-perfect "had made" makes this backward glance clear in English. "Very good" (*tov me'od*) is a heightening of the refrain "good" used on the earlier days, and the adverb is placed after the adjective in Hebrew for emphasis. The dash before "the sixth day" reflects that the Hebrew simply juxtaposes the day-label without a verb or preposition; the dash lets the phrase land as a closing beat when read aloud.

*Tov* covers what is beautiful, fitting, useful and morally right, so "good" here is broader than ethical goodness; *me'od* originally means "muchness, force" and functions as an intensifier. The refrain of the chapter uses *tov* seven times, with this final occurrence alone intensified. Notably, the numeral in *yom hashishi* carries the definite article ("the sixth day"), unlike days two through five, which are anarthrous ("a second day" and so on); the same definiteness marks the seventh day, drawing the two closing days together as the goal of the sequence. *Asah* ("make, do") is used here rather than *bara* ("create"), the two verbs alternating throughout the chapter as near synonyms for God's creative work.

The verdict "very good" is a cornerstone of biblical teaching about creation: the material world, embodied life, sexual difference, food and fruitfulness are affirmed as God's own valuation, not merely tolerated. Interpreters have long read this against dualistic views that treat matter or the body as evil. "Very good" is not the same as "perfect" or "incapable of change": readers differ on whether the phrase describes a completed, flawless state or a world well-made and ready for its purpose, with human vocation and history still ahead. The evaluation covers "all that he had made," including the great sea creatures and the darkness and deep of the opening verses, which elsewhere in the ancient world were figures of chaos or menace.

The day is reckoned from evening to morning, matching a calendar in which the new day begins at sunset — the practice reflected in Israel's festivals and Sabbath observance. The sixth day is the last working day; in the surrounding cultures creation accounts often culminated in the building of a temple or the rest of the gods, and the reader who knows the pattern will expect the seventh day that follows. Other ancient Near Eastern creation stories present humanity as an afterthought or as labor for the gods, whereas here the day that includes humankind receives the intensified verdict.

The Hebrew manuscript tradition is uniform here; a paragraph marker (*petuchah*) closes the verse, dividing the six days from the account of the seventh. The Greek tradition reads the evaluation as a plural, "and behold, all things were very good," agreeing with "all that he had made" rather than with an implied singular; some Greek witnesses also add the formula found earlier in the chapter. These are stylistic harmonizations rather than evidence of a different Hebrew text.

The closing words "the sixth day" begin the Sabbath-eve blessing over wine in Jewish practice, which joins them to the following account of the seventh day; the phrase thus functions liturgically as an opening rather than an ending. In Christian worship the six-day account with its refrain of goodness is a standard reading at the vigil of Easter and at services of thanksgiving for creation, and the "very good" verdict is frequently used as a call to worship or as an offertory sentence.
